name: Gentian Blue
lede: Gentian Blue is a strong purplish blue named for the gentian flower, listed by Ridgway in 1912 and the ISCC-NBS in 1955.

sections.title: A flower and an old list
sections.body:
In the Werner color nomenclature as Syme edited it, the gentian is an example under two blues: the back parts of the flower under China blue, and the flower itself under azure blue [1]. Baty reproduces the list with its animal, vegetable and mineral examples [1].

Our library carries *gentian blue* in Ridgway's standards of 1912 (plate XXI), in a German RAL list of 1927, in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary and in the ISCC-NBS of 1955 [2]. Measured against the ISCC-NBS categories, the swatch is nearest to strong purplish blue, 5.7 units of ΔE2000 away [2]. Nearby are [[periwinkle]], [[cornflower]] and [[pearl-gentian]].

sections.title: Not gentian violet
sections.body: Garfield lists gentian violet among dyes that became drugs, employed against bacteria and fungi [3]. It is a dye, not the flower, so do not confuse it with the blue of the petals.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This tone is rare in our archive: 9 paintings, 0.04 per cent, as photographed [4]. The earliest is by Cesare da Sesto, from 1517 [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [4].

origin.first_recorded: Werner and Syme nomenclature (undated here); Ridgway 1912

field.dataset: ColorHub archive of about 23,800 paintings, as photographed

questions.q: Which part of the gentian flower is a China blue example in the Werner list Baty reproduces?
What does Garfield say gentian violet was employed for?

openers: Gentian was already a model blue in the Werner nomenclature as Syme edited it.

issues: Removed claim that gentian violet is a different color from the flower; Garfield only lists it as an antibacterial and antifungal dye.
